WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Throughout her career, singer-songwriter Cyndi Lauper has promoted gay and lesbian rights. She has a personal connection to this cause -- her sister is a lesbian -- but she also believes it's a matter of fairness. Cyndi Lauper worked with Cathy Nelson of the Human Rights Campaign to raise awareness of LGBT issues. "It's always wrong to discriminate," the Grammy Award winner said. "I grew up in the civil rights movement. It was wrong then, and it is wrong now." With her 2007 and 2008 "True Colors" tours, Lauper has helped raise awareness about lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender rights around the country. She said fellow LGBT activist Cathy Nelson especially motivates her. Nelson worked at the Human Rights Campaign (HRC), a national LGBT civil rights organization, and her dedication to those issues runs deep. Fighting for fairness and equality, she said, drives her. "I'm a lesbian, and I see the issues very personally," Nelson said. "When it deep-down resonates that you don't have the same rights and responsibilities, or people don't view you the same, it can be demoralizing and empowering at the same time." Nelson's passion for the cause has enabled her to inspire thousands of people across the country to get involved. When she was growing up in rural Illinois, Nelson said, she hadn't imagined following this path. She trained to be a teacher, but on a whim, became a flight attendant with Eastern Airlines to fulfill her "intense desire to travel." In the 1980s, she became involved with labor issues through her flight attendant union. That led to working on women's issues with the National Organization of Women in Washington. In 1989, she started working for the HRC. Since then, she has helped bring LGBT rights out of the closet and onto the national stage. Hired to increase the group's membership, Nelson built a strong volunteer network in communities across the nation. HRC had just 12,000 members when Nelson started. Today it has more than 725,000, making it the largest gay and lesbian rights organization in the country. "Part of my job is getting people to be vocal," Nelson said. "It's important that everyone has an understanding that discrimination is happening every single day against a certain segment of society. And that's just wrong." In 2007, when Lauper worked with HRC for the "True Colors" tour, she and Nelson teamed up to bring gay and straight audiences together on fairness and equality issues. Nelson realized it was also an opportunity to shine the spotlight on an issue she'd worked on for almost a decade -- the passage of a hate crimes bill that would make attacks based on sexual orientation, disability, or gender a federal crime. For Nelson, crimes against LGBT people -- such as the murder of Matthew Shepard -- represent the darkest side of ignorance on these issues. In 2006, more than one in six hate crimes were committed against LGBT individuals, an 18 percent rise over the previous year, according to the FBI. "I learned from Cathy that hate crimes send fear through a community," Lauper said. "You could die just because of who you are."  Watch Lauper and Nelson talk about the "True Colors" tour to raise awareness » . At every concert, Lauper spoke passionately about the need to pass the bill, and her song, "True Colors," was used in a public service announcement about the legislation. HRC volunteers distributed information at each venue and had postcards on hand for people to send to their legislators. In the end, more than 15,000 people signed postcards, and both houses of Congress passed the bill by wide margins. Although President Bush never signed the bill, Nelson and Lauper have high hopes for it to soon become law. For Nelson, getting so many people engaged was a key achievement. "The biggest reward for me is when I've played some part in empowering someone to get involved," she said. Lauper knows first-hand how convincing Nelson can be. "The fact that you can actually succeed and help people -- you really get that from her," she said. "People like Cathy get all of us motivated."

Lauper’s 2007 and 2008 “True Colors” concert tours drew nationwide attention to the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people. She identified Nelson, another LGBT advocate, as a particularly important source of inspiration.

Nelson worked for the Human Rights Campaign, a national civil rights organization focused on LGBT people. Her commitment to equality was deeply personal. As a lesbian, she said she directly experienced what it meant to lack equal rights and responsibilities or to be regarded differently by others. That realization, she explained, could simultaneously feel discouraging and spur someone into action.

Through her dedication, Nelson encouraged thousands of Americans to participate in the movement. Yet while growing up in rural Illinois, she never expected her life to take this direction. She initially studied to become a teacher. Later, acting on impulse and driven by a powerful wish to see the world, she became a flight attendant for Eastern Airlines.

During the 1980s, Nelson’s flight attendants’ union introduced her to labor activism. That experience eventually led her to Washington, where she worked on women’s causes with the National Organization for Women. She joined the Human Rights Campaign in 1989 and subsequently helped move LGBT equality from a largely hidden subject into the national conversation.

Nelson was originally recruited to expand HRC’s membership. To do so, she developed an extensive network of volunteers in communities throughout the United States. The organization had only 12,000 members when she arrived; it later grew to more than 725,000, becoming the nation’s largest organization supporting gay and lesbian rights.

Nelson said an important part of her role was encouraging people to speak out. She wanted the public to recognize that one group in society faces discrimination every day—and that such treatment is fundamentally unjust.

When Lauper partnered with HRC for the 2007 “True Colors” tour, she and Nelson used the events to unite gay and straight audiences around equality and fairness. Lauper said Nelson taught her that hate crimes create fear throughout an entire community. Such violence means a person could be killed simply for being who they are. Lauper and Nelson also appeared in a video discussing how the “True Colors” tour promoted awareness.

At every performance, Lauper strongly urged passage of the proposed law. Her song “True Colors” appeared in a public-service announcement supporting the measure. Meanwhile, HRC volunteers provided educational materials at each concert location and supplied postcards that attendees could mail to their lawmakers.

Ultimately, over 15,000 people signed the postcards. The legislation won decisive approval in both chambers of Congress, though President George W. Bush did not sign it. Even so, Lauper and Nelson remained optimistic that it would soon become law.

# Lauper, Nelson turn ‘True Colors’ into a call for equality

**By CNN**

Cyndi Lauper has long used her unmistakable voice to celebrate people who refuse to hide who they are. Through the “True Colors” tours, the Grammy-winning singer found a partner in Human Rights Campaign activist Cathy Nelson, helping transform a series of summer concerts into a traveling campaign for LGBT equality.

The tours paired music, comedy and political organizing, bringing together performers and advocates in cities across North America. Artists including Lauper, Erasure, Debbie Harry, the B-52s and comedian Margaret Cho appeared on various lineups, while the Human Rights Campaign used the events to connect concertgoers with its work on anti-discrimination protections, relationship recognition and other equality issues.

For Lauper, whose 1986 ballad “True Colors” became an anthem of acceptance, the cause was personal as well as political. She has often spoken about friends and family members in the LGBT community and about the discrimination they faced. The tour offered a way to make advocacy feel welcoming rather than remote — delivering a civil-rights message between familiar songs and flashes of pop spectacle.

Nelson helped provide the organizing link. Working with the Human Rights Campaign, one of the country’s largest LGBT civil-rights organizations, she helped ensure that the tour was more than a symbolic show of support. HRC representatives attended stops, shared information and encouraged fans to become involved after the final encore.

That partnership reflected a simple division of strengths: Lauper could draw an audience and speak through popular culture; Nelson and HRC could turn the energy in the crowd into sustained political engagement.

The project arrived at a time when LGBT Americans faced a sharply uneven legal landscape. Same-sex couples lacked federal marriage recognition, workplace protections varied widely, and debates over military service and hate-crimes laws remained national flash points. The “True Colors” platform placed those issues before audiences who might not attend a rally or policy forum.

Yet the concerts were designed as celebrations, not lectures. The atmosphere was bright, theatrical and deliberately inclusive. Comedy shared the stage with dance music, rock and Lauper’s own catalog, including “Girls Just Want to Have Fun,” “Time After Time” and the song that gave the tour its name.

That balance was central to the effort. Lauper’s public role made equality vivid and emotional; Nelson’s activism connected that emotion to the practical work of changing laws and attitudes.

Together, they showed how a concert tour could become a mobile community — part entertainment event, part organizing drive and part declaration that people should be able to live openly without fear.

The message echoed the song at its center: Equality begins when people are seen, and valued, in their true colors.

# Cyndi Lauper, Cathy Nelson, and the Campaign for Federal LGBT Protections

Cyndi Lauper’s LGBT advocacy grew from personal solidarity into a sustained program of political organizing, fundraising, and public education. Although she was best known as the singer behind “Girls Just Want to Have Fun” and “Time After Time,” Lauper increasingly used another of her signature songs—“True Colors”—as the emotional center of a movement. Her work brought together entertainers, veteran organizers such as Cathy Nelson, and national groups including the Human Rights Campaign at a time when LGBT organizations were trying to convert cultural visibility into federal law.

That collaboration was especially evident in the True Colors concert tours of the late 2000s. The tours helped raise money and awareness for LGBT organizations, build pressure for federal hate-crimes legislation, and demonstrate that support for equality could mobilize a broad mainstream audience.

## Advocacy rooted in family and experience

Lauper has often connected her commitment to LGBT rights to her family, particularly her relationship with her lesbian sister, Ellen. She has also described growing up around people who experienced rejection because they did not conform to conventional expectations about sexuality or gender.

These experiences made LGBT equality more than a celebrity cause for her. By the 1980s and 1990s, when AIDS, political hostility, and social stigma were defining much of LGBT public life, Lauper was visibly welcoming to gay audiences and resistant to efforts to marginalize them. “True Colors,” released in 1986, was not written specifically as an LGBT anthem, but its message of dignity and self-revelation was widely embraced by LGBT listeners.

Lauper eventually turned that symbolic connection into organized advocacy. She participated in benefits, spoke publicly for equality, and worked with national organizations rather than limiting her involvement to occasional statements of support.

## Cathy Nelson’s organizing role

Cathy Nelson was important to this transition from goodwill to organized political action. A longtime LGBT fundraiser and strategist, Nelson had deep experience with the Human Rights Campaign and with building national donor networks. She understood how to turn public enthusiasm into mailing lists, contributions, local participation, and pressure on elected officials.

Nelson had worked during the formative period of the Human Rights Campaign Fund, as HRC was originally known. The organization began in 1980 primarily as a political action committee focused on directing money to candidates supportive of gay and lesbian rights. Over time, it developed into a broader membership, lobbying, communications, and public-education organization.

Fundraising professionals such as Nelson helped make that expansion possible. Direct-mail campaigns, recurring-giving programs, major-donor networks, and benefit events enabled HRC to reach beyond a relatively small circle of Washington activists. Its donor and supporter base grew from the tens of thousands in its early years to a national constituency eventually counted in the hundreds of thousands. HRC later reported even larger totals by combining members, donors, and supporters, though those categories were not always equivalent to dues-paying membership.

Nelson’s partnership with Lauper drew on both women’s strengths. Lauper could attract press attention and audiences that conventional lobbying campaigns might not reach. Nelson could connect that attention to organizations, legislative goals, and long-term fundraising. Their work illustrates a recurring pattern in LGBT advocacy: celebrity visibility is most politically effective when joined to professional organizing.

## The True Colors tours

The clearest expression of that partnership was the True Colors touring project, launched in 2007. The tour featured Lauper alongside a rotating group of performers and personalities, many of them openly LGBT or strongly associated with LGBT audiences. Participants over the tours included Erasure, Debbie Harry, the Dresden Dolls, the Gossip, Joan Jett, the B-52s, the Indigo Girls, and comedian and host Margaret Cho.

The concerts combined entertainment with political messaging. Audiences received information about discrimination, voting, and pending legislation. LGBT organizations were given opportunities to recruit supporters, distribute materials, and encourage direct action. A portion of ticket proceeds benefited HRC and other organizations associated with the campaign.

The name “True Colors” was particularly effective. To many LGBT people, the song already expressed the courage required to live openly. Lauper and her partners transformed that emotional identification into a public platform organized around equality.

The tour also expanded the conventional audience for LGBT politics. Rather than speaking only to activists at conferences or donors at formal dinners, it reached music fans in cities across the country. Its roster mixed queer performers with mainstream popular acts, presenting LGBT rights not as a narrow interest but as a question of civil rights and basic fairness.

## HRC’s evolution into a national political force

The Human Rights Campaign’s involvement reflected how much the organization had changed since its founding. Initially, the Human Rights Campaign Fund concentrated on campaign contributions and access to federal lawmakers. As the AIDS crisis, military discrimination, anti-gay ballot initiatives, and debates over marriage intensified, HRC developed a wider institutional structure.

By the 1990s and 2000s, HRC had become one of the country’s largest LGBT advocacy groups. It maintained a substantial Washington lobbying operation, published congressional scorecards, endorsed candidates, organized members in key states and districts, and invested heavily in advertising and public education.

Its growth gave LGBT advocates a larger presence in federal politics, but it also generated criticism. Grassroots activists sometimes viewed HRC as too closely tied to Washington elites, too cautious about direct action, or too willing to compromise. Transgender advocates also criticized periods when national organizations did not consistently insist on fully inclusive legislation. Those debates became particularly intense during the 2007 fight over the Employment Non-Discrimination Act, when a version lacking gender-identity protections divided the movement.

The True Colors project helped HRC address at least part of the distance between institutional politics and popular activism. A touring concert could carry a federal legislative message into communities far beyond Capitol Hill, while HRC supplied the campaign infrastructure needed to follow up with lawmakers.

## The struggle for federal hate-crimes legislation

One of the central legislative goals promoted through this advocacy was passage of a federal hate-crimes law that explicitly covered crimes motivated by sexual orientation and gender identity.

Federal hate-crimes law already allowed national authorities to intervene in certain bias-motivated crimes, but its reach was limited. Existing law concentrated largely on race, color, religion, and national origin and often required proof that the victim had been engaged in a federally protected activity, such as voting or attending school.

The murders of Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. in 1998 gave the movement for stronger legislation new urgency. Shepard, a gay college student in Wyoming, was beaten, tied to a fence, and left to die. Byrd, a Black man in Texas, was murdered by white supremacists who dragged him behind a truck. Their deaths became symbols of the deadly consequences of bias and of gaps in federal law.

Over the following decade, versions of expanded hate-crimes legislation repeatedly passed one chamber of Congress or were attached to larger bills, only to stall, be removed, or face veto threats. Supporters sought to:

- Add sexual orientation, gender identity, gender, and disability to the protected categories.
- Remove the requirement that a victim be participating in a narrowly defined federally protected activity.
- Allow federal authorities to assist state and local investigations.
- Provide grants and technical support to local law-enforcement agencies.
- Permit federal prosecution when local authorities were unable or unwilling to act.

Opponents argued that such laws punished thought or threatened religious speech. Supporters responded that hate-crimes statutes punished criminal conduct, not belief or expression, and that motive had long been considered in criminal law when determining the nature and seriousness of an offense.

## Lauper’s role in the legislative campaign

Lauper used concerts, interviews, public-service messages, and appearances connected with HRC to draw attention to the legislation. The purpose was not merely to express sympathy for victims. Audiences were urged to contact members of Congress and to treat passage of the bill as an achievable political objective.

Her value to the campaign was partly communicative. Legislative language about jurisdiction, protected categories, and federal assistance could seem remote to the general public. Lauper framed the issue in moral terms: people should not be attacked because of who they are, and the federal government should be able to respond when bias crimes overwhelm or escape local justice.

The True Colors tours also helped keep gender identity visible within the campaign. This mattered because transgender protections were politically vulnerable and because transgender people—particularly transgender women of color—faced high levels of violence. An inclusive hate-crimes bill demonstrated that a national LGBT coalition could press for protections extending beyond sexual orientation alone.

At the same time, Lauper’s involvement did not replace the work of victims’ families, legal advocates, congressional sponsors, local organizations, and full-time lobbyists. The campaign succeeded through a division of labor. Public figures generated attention; organizers such as Nelson built networks and resources; HRC and allied groups lobbied Congress; and families including those of Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. gave the legislation enduring moral force.

## Passage of the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Act

After years of failed efforts, Congress passed the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act in 2009 as part of a larger defense authorization measure. President Barack Obama signed it into law on October 28, 2009.

The law expanded federal authority over hate crimes and explicitly included crimes motivated by a victim’s actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender, or disability. It also strengthened the federal government’s ability to support state and local investigations.

Passage was a major victory, but it did not end anti-LGBT violence. Hate-crimes statutes operate after an offense has occurred, and enforcement can vary. Victims may hesitate to report attacks, police departments may classify incidents inconsistently, and prosecutors still must prove the required bias motivation. The law therefore represented both a substantive legal change and a statement that violence directed at LGBT people was a national civil-rights concern.

## From True Colors to youth homelessness

Lauper’s advocacy continued beyond the hate-crimes fight. In 2008 she helped establish the True Colors Fund, now known as True Colors United. The organization focuses on homelessness among LGBTQ youth, who are disproportionately represented in the youth homeless population, often because of family rejection, discrimination, or unsafe home environments.

This work reflected an evolution in Lauper’s activism. The True Colors tours had emphasized visibility, coalition-building, and federal legislation. The new organization concentrated on policy and systems affecting young people without stable housing. It worked with service providers, communities, and public agencies to make homeless services safer and more responsive to LGBTQ youth.

That shift also showed the lasting significance of her partnership with professional organizers. Rather than creating a short-lived celebrity charity, Lauper helped build an institution intended to operate beyond concert cycles and individual legislative campaigns.

## A model of culture joined to organizing

Cyndi Lauper’s contribution to LGBT advocacy cannot be measured solely by money raised or bills passed. Her larger achievement was to connect culture with political infrastructure.

“True Colors” gave the movement an accessible language of openness and self-worth. Cathy Nelson and other experienced organizers helped translate that language into fundraising, coalition-building, and action. HRC’s expanding national network provided a channel through which concertgoers and admirers could become donors, voters, and constituents. The long campaign for the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act supplied a concrete legislative objective.

The partnership was therefore more than a singer lending her name to a cause. It was an example of how social movements grow: personal conviction attracts public attention; organizers build durable institutions; institutions focus pressure on government; and cultural affirmation becomes part of a campaign for enforceable rights.

Lauper remained the recognizable face of that effort, but its effectiveness depended on the less visible work of Nelson, HRC staff members, local activists, victims’ families, performers, donors, and audiences. Together, they helped move LGBT equality from the margins of American politics toward the center of the national civil-rights debate.

# People Who Motivate Us: Cathy Nelson Helped Cyndi Lauper Turn Applause Into Action

*The veteran activist persuaded the pop singer that a concert crowd could be more than an audience—it could be a constituency for gay and lesbian equality.*

**By Staff Writer**

For years, Cyndi Lauper had spoken openly about gay and lesbian rights. The singer’s connection to the issue was personal: her sister, Ellen, is a lesbian, and gay fans had supported Lauper since “Girls Just Want to Have Fun” made her a star in the 1980s.

But it was activist Cathy Nelson who helped Lauper see how much more she could do.

Nelson urged the singer to look beyond making supportive statements and consider the thousands of people already gathered at her concerts. Those fans, Nelson suggested, could be informed, registered and mobilized. A night of music could also become an organizing opportunity.

The idea stayed with Lauper. She began using her platform not simply to celebrate the gay community, but to connect audiences with organizations working for legal and political change. That approach became especially visible through the True Colors concert tours, launched in 2007 and continued in 2008.

Featuring performers and entertainers including Erasure, Debbie Harry, the B-52s, the Indigo Girls, Rosie O’Donnell and Wanda Sykes, the tours mixed pop spectacle with a clear civil-rights message. Concertgoers could learn about issues facing lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender Americans, meet representatives of advocacy groups and find ways to participate after the final encore.

The Human Rights Campaign joined the effort, helping turn tour stops into opportunities for outreach and political engagement. The concerts called attention to workplace discrimination, hate-crimes protections and the continuing struggle for equal treatment of same-sex couples.

## Cathy Nelson: From Rural Illinois to a National Voice for Equality

Cathy Nelson’s career in social justice began far from Washington’s political institutions. Raised in rural Illinois, she came of age in a community where lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people were rarely visible and seldom discussed openly. That background gave Nelson a lasting appreciation for the isolation many LGBTQ people experience—and for the power of visibility to change attitudes.

As a young adult, Nelson became a flight attendant with Eastern Airlines. The job took her beyond the confines of small-town Illinois and introduced her to a diverse workforce, organized labor and the practical realities of discrimination. During Eastern’s turbulent labor struggles, she gained experience in collective action, communications and mobilizing people around a shared cause. Those skills became the foundation of her later advocacy.

Nelson moved into the women’s movement through the National Organization for Women. At NOW, she worked on organizing and public education at a time when the organization was increasingly confronting lesbian rights, reproductive freedom, workplace equality and the political power of the religious right. She learned how to translate personal experiences into persuasive public messages and how to connect LGBTQ equality with the broader struggle for women’s civil rights.

She later brought that experience to the Human Rights Campaign, where she became a prominent communications strategist and spokesperson. Nelson helped HRC present LGBTQ people and their families not as abstractions in a political debate, but as neighbors, coworkers and citizens seeking equal treatment. Her work encompassed employment protections, relationship recognition, political organizing and efforts to secure stronger federal responses to bias-motivated violence.

A particularly visible chapter of Nelson’s career was her collaboration with singer and longtime LGBTQ ally Cyndi Lauper. Nelson helped connect Lauper’s celebrity and personal commitment to organized equality campaigns, including the **True Colors** initiative. Through concerts, public appearances, media outreach and partnerships with advocacy organizations, they used popular culture to reach audiences that conventional political campaigns often missed.

Their work also emphasized hate-crime awareness. Lauper and Nelson spoke publicly about the human consequences of anti-LGBTQ violence and supported efforts associated with federal hate-crimes protections, including the campaign that culminated in the Matthew Shepard and James Byrd Jr. Hate Crimes Prevention Act. The message was both political and personal: prejudice was not merely offensive rhetoric; it could produce exclusion, homelessness and deadly violence.

Nelson’s journey—from rural Illinois and Eastern Airlines to NOW, HRC and the True Colors movement—illustrates how labor organizing, feminism, LGBTQ advocacy and popular culture can reinforce one another. Her distinctive contribution has been communications: making equality understandable, emotionally immediate and difficult for the wider public to ignore.
